title: Grow Your Relationship: 8 Milestones That Bring You Closer
h1: Grow Your Relationship: 8 Shared Milestones That Bring You Closer
description: Want to grow your relationship? Learn how first dates, first fights, first trips and other shared milestones build trust, and how to make each one count.
excerpt: First dates, first fights, first trips: how the milestones you share can deepen trust, and what to do at each stage to grow your relationship on purpose.
intro:
Relationships don't grow in a straight line. They grow in moments: the first date that ran three hours long, the first argument you actually resolved, the first trip where you saw each other tired, hungry and lost. Each of those experiences teaches you something about your partner and about the two of you as a team.

If you want to grow your relationship intentionally rather than just hoping it deepens on its own, it helps to recognize these milestones and make the most of them. Below are eight shared experiences that tend to shape couples, what each one can teach you, and practical ways to turn them into lasting closeness.
body:
Why shared experiences help a relationship grow

Closeness is built from two ingredients: time and meaning. Spending time together matters, but the moments that really bond couples are the ones that ask something of you. You have to communicate, compromise, show up or be vulnerable. Those moments create shared stories, and shared stories become the foundation of a "we."

Relationship researcher John Gottman describes "bids for connection," the small ways partners reach for each other's attention, such as pointing out something funny or asking for help. Couples who regularly turn toward those bids, rather than ignoring them, tend to build more trust. Big milestones are basically a concentrated version of the same thing: a chance to turn toward each other when it counts.

Early milestones: getting to know each other

The first months are about discovery. You are learning how the other person thinks, what they care about and whether you feel safe being yourself around them.

1. The first real date

Your first date sets the tone. It's less about the perfect restaurant and more about whether you can be curious, relaxed and honest with each other.

  • What it teaches you: Whether conversation flows, whether you feel at ease, and whether you both want more.
  • How to grow from it: Ask questions that go beyond small talk and actually listen to the answers. Afterward, follow up with something specific you enjoyed ("I'm still laughing about your road trip story").

Need help keeping things flowing? Our list of first date questions and the follow-up guide to second date questions are a great place to start.

2. The first time you say how you feel

Whether it's "I really like you," "I don't want to see anyone else" or "I love you," the first declaration is a leap of trust. One person goes first, and that takes courage.

  • What it teaches you: How your partner responds to vulnerability, and whether you're moving at a similar pace.
  • How to grow from it: Say it when you mean it, not to get a particular response. If you're on the receiving end and not quite there yet, respond with honesty and warmth: "I care about you a lot, and I'm so glad you told me."

Not sure whether what you're feeling is love? Read how do you know you're in love.

Milestones that test you as a team

These are the moments that ask something of you. They can feel uncomfortable while they are happening, but they often do the most to deepen trust, because they show you how you both act under pressure.

3. The first obstacle or argument

Every couple eventually disagrees. The first serious conflict can feel scary, but it's also one of the most valuable milestones you'll have, because it shows you how you repair.

  • What it teaches you: Whether you can disagree without contempt, whether you both apologize, and whether the argument ends with more understanding or just silence.
  • How to grow from it: Focus on the problem, not the person. Use "I" statements ("I felt left out when plans changed") instead of accusations ("You never think about me"). Take a break if things get heated, then come back to finish the conversation.
Tip: After any significant disagreement, do a short "repair talk" once you're both calm: What did each of you need in that moment? What would help next time? Couples who repair well often feel closer after a conflict than before it.

4. The first trip together

Travel strips away routines. You'll see how your partner handles delays, budgets, unfamiliar places and too much togetherness.

  • What it teaches you: Whether you plan well together, how you each handle stress, and how much alone time each of you needs.
  • How to grow from it: Start with a short weekend away rather than two weeks abroad. Talk in advance about budget, pace and must-dos. Build in a little solo time, and laugh at the things that go wrong; they often become your favorite stories.

5. Meeting each other's people

Meeting friends and family shows you where your partner comes from and lets you into the wider circle of their life.

  • What it teaches you: How your partner acts around the people who know them best, and how well your social worlds fit together.
  • How to grow from it: Prepare each other with a little background ("My uncle loves to debate, don't take the bait"). Afterward, debrief kindly. Avoid criticizing their loved ones harshly, even if the evening was awkward.

6. Supporting each other through a hard time

A job loss, a health scare, a family crisis or a period of stress will eventually show up. How you support each other through it is one of the clearest tests of a partnership.

  • What it teaches you: Whether you can lean on each other, and whether you know how your partner prefers to be supported.
  • How to grow from it: Ask, "Do you want me to help solve this, or do you just need me to listen?" Offer practical help like meals or errands. And remember that the supporting partner needs care too.

Milestones of commitment

As the relationship matures, milestones shift from discovering each other to choosing each other on purpose. These moments are about looking back with gratitude and forward with shared intention.

7. Your first anniversary

An anniversary is a natural moment to look back at how far you've come and look ahead at what you want.

  • What it teaches you: What you both value, and whether you're growing in the same direction.
  • How to grow from it: Celebrate in a way that feels like you, whether that's a fancy dinner, recreating your first date or a quiet night in. Then talk: What was your favorite memory this year? What do you want more of next year? For heartfelt words, browse our anniversary wishes.

8. Making a bigger commitment

Moving in, getting a pet, merging finances, getting engaged: each bigger commitment intertwines your lives in a new way.

  • What it teaches you: How you make big decisions together and handle the practical side of a shared life.
  • How to grow from it: Talk about expectations before you commit. Who handles which chores? How will you split costs? What happens when you need space? Clear agreements now prevent resentment later.

Everyday habits that keep your relationship growing

Milestones are memorable, but the ordinary days between them do most of the work. A few simple habits help:

  • Daily check-ins. Ten minutes of phone-free conversation about your days keeps you connected.
  • Regular dates. Keep dating each other, even when life gets busy. Novelty helps, so try new activities now and then.
  • Appreciation out loud. Notice the small things your partner does and thank them specifically.
  • Learning each other's love language. Some people feel loved through words, others through time, touch, help or gifts. Our guide on how to show love has practical ideas.
  • Growing as individuals. Healthy couples give each other room to pursue friendships, goals and hobbies. Two growing people make a growing relationship.
Tip: Once a month, ask each other: "What's one thing I could do that would make you feel more loved this month?" It takes two minutes and often reveals easy wins.

When growth feels stuck

Sometimes a relationship plateaus. You're comfortable, but you're not getting closer. That's normal, and it doesn't mean something is wrong. Try introducing something new: a shared class, a trip, a project or a fresh tradition. Talk honestly about what you each miss. If the same conflicts keep coming up without resolution, a licensed couples therapist can help you find new ways forward. More ideas live in our relationships section.

The bottom line

You grow your relationship by treating milestones as chances to learn about each other, and by showing up consistently in between. Celebrate the firsts, repair after the hard moments, keep talking about what you both want, and keep choosing each other. That's how a connection becomes a partnership.
takeaways: Shared experiences, especially challenging ones, build trust and a sense of "we."
How you repair after your first argument matters more than avoiding conflict.
Travel, meeting family and hard times reveal how you work as a team.
Use anniversaries and big commitments to talk openly about expectations and goals.
Small daily habits like check-ins and appreciation keep the relationship growing between milestones.

faq.q: How do you grow a relationship with your partner?
faq.a: Spend intentional time together, communicate openly, and treat shared milestones such as trips, disagreements and anniversaries as chances to learn about each other. Daily habits matter too: phone-free check-ins, regular dates, specific appreciation and giving each other room to grow as individuals all help a relationship deepen over time.

faq.q: What are the stages of a growing relationship?
faq.a: Many couples move through early attraction, getting to know each other, a first real disagreement, deeper trust and commitment, and building a shared life. The order and timing vary for every couple. What matters is that both people keep communicating and repairing along the way rather than following a set timeline.

faq.q: Is it normal for a relationship to feel stagnant?
faq.a: Yes, most long-term relationships have flat periods. Trying something new together, talking honestly about what each of you misses, and reintroducing regular dates often helps. If the same conflicts keep recurring or one of you feels unhappy for a long time, a licensed couples therapist can be a useful support.

faq.q: How soon should you go on a trip with a new partner?
faq.a: There is no set rule, but many couples start with a short weekend away once they feel comfortable and have talked about budget and expectations. A shorter trip lets you see how you travel together without too much pressure, and you can plan something longer once you know you enjoy it.
